stem: A client arrives with ongoing chest pressure that began about 1 hour ago. The initial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin is not elevated. Which nursing interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The single early troponin result excludes acute myocardial infarction, so further cardiac evaluation is unnecessary.
options.B: The client should continue the acute coronary syndrome evaluation, including serial high-sensitivity troponin testing according to the facility’s validated clinical pathway.
options.C: A normal initial troponin establishes a noncardiac cause of the chest pressure even if symptoms persist.
options.D: Troponin testing has little role in acute chest-pain evaluation unless ST-segment elevation is already present on the ECG.

rationale: B is correct. High-sensitivity cardiac troponin is the preferred biomarker for myocardial injury, but interpretation depends on symptom timing, the assay, serial change, ECG findings, and the overall clinical picture. Rapid rule-out strategies can be unreliable in very early presenters because troponin may not yet have risen; therefore an initial non-elevated result obtained about 1 hour after symptom onset does not by itself exclude myocardial infarction. A and C incorrectly treat one early value as definitive. D is incorrect because serial high-sensitivity troponin is central to evaluating suspected acute coronary syndrome even when ST-segment elevation is absent.
educational_objective: Do not use a single non-elevated high-sensitivity troponin obtained very early after symptom onset to rule out myocardial infarction; continue serial troponin assessment and clinical/ECG evaluation using a validated chest-pain pathway.
source_organization: American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association
source_document_title: 2021 AHA/ACC Guideline for the Evaluation and Diagnosis of Chest Pain; 2022 ACC Expert Consensus Decision Pathway on Acute Chest Pain
source_version_date: Chest Pain Guideline published 2021; ACC expert consensus published 2022; currentness checked against 2025 ACC/AHA Acute Coronary Syndromes guideline; accessed 2026-08-17
source_locator: 2021 Chest Pain Guideline Perspectives — serial assessment of cardiac troponin I or T is the preferred biomarker strategy and high-sensitivity cTn is preferred; 2022 ACC Expert Consensus key points — serial hs-cTn measurements are essential for MI confirmation and rapid hs-cTn algorithms can fail in very early presenters; interpretation depends on symptom onset and clinical data
source_claim_supported: A single non-elevated high-sensitivity troponin obtained very early after symptom onset cannot independently exclude acute MI; serial hs-cTn testing integrated with timing, ECG, and clinical assessment is the recommended approach in suspected ACS.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential; monitor diagnostic tests and recognize abnormal or evolving findings; Physiological Adaptation — recognize complications and manage acute cardiovascular conditions
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — serial troponin interpretation in suspected acute coronary syndrome
correction_summary: Rebuilt the source item because ‘normal troponin several hours after symptom onset’ is assay- and timing-dependent and could make serial testing nonessential in selected validated rule-out pathways. The final item specifies a very early presentation, where one normal hs-cTn cannot safely rule out MI, and avoids inventing a universal repeat interval.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.clinical_category: acute coronary syndrome / cardiac biomarker interpretation
audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against official ACC/AHA chest-pain guidance and ACC expert consensus. The sources support serial hs-cTn assessment, preference for hs-cTn, and caution that rapid algorithms may fail in patients presenting very early after symptom onset. Currentness was checked against the 2025 ACS guideline hub.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: The stem uses a clearly early 1-hour presentation so the non-elevated initial hs-cTn cannot be treated as definitive. B directs continued evaluation without prescribing an assay-independent sampling interval. The rationale does not claim every patient requires identical serial timing.
audit_findings.choice_A: Incorrect. A single early non-elevated hs-cTn does not independently exclude MI.
audit_findings.choice_B: Correct. Serial hs-cTn within a validated pathway plus ECG/clinical context is appropriate for an early presenter.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect. A normal early troponin does not establish a noncardiac diagnosis.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect. Troponin is central to suspected ACS assessment even without ST-segment elevation.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B accounts for the very early timing and need for a validated serial pathway. The item avoids the later-presenter scenario in which a single very low hs-cTn may be sufficient under specific assay/pathway conditions.
audit_findings.cueing: All four options are interpretations/actions concerning troponin-based ACS evaluation; the correct response is not uniquely long or technically worded relative to the construct.
audit_findings.blueprint: Reduction of Risk Potential is appropriate because the nurse is interpreting a diagnostic biomarker in a time-sensitive acute condition to avoid a missed complication.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Re-audited symptom-onset timing, hs-cTn assay dependence, single-sample rule-out exceptions, serial testing, ECG integration, 2025 guideline currentness, second-answer risk, and NCLEX scope. No unresolved conflict remained.
